1093.title: A hymn in Tilang
1093.hook: Tilang holds Guru Nanak's hymn to Lalo about Babur's invasion, and its promise of a time for truth
1093.howItsDone: Guru Nanak's Tilang hymn addressed to Bhai Lalo is sung in kirtan in Raga Tilang, and its line about speaking as the Master's word comes is quoted by some Sikhs as a standard for honest speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Tilang, where Guru Nanak's plea leans toward Persian. Your line: persian color. A new week starts.

When is the right time to say a hard, true thing? Right away, while it's raw? Later, when it's safe? Only to the people in charge? A page into the Tilang section, Guru Nanak gives his answer in the middle of a disaster. An army has come down from Kabul. Wedding songs have turned into songs of blood. And the hymn is addressed to one man by name, again and again: Lalo. Today: a hymn in Tilang, and what it does with the truth.
screen: `WHEN DO YOU SAY THE HARD THING?` → `AN ARMY FROM KABUL.` → `ADDRESSED TO LALO.`

segments.voice: Earlier on this path you heard this shabad as courage, and as a word told first to a working man. Today, watch its moves. First, it names what went missing. In paraphrase: modesty and dharma have both hidden themselves, and falsehood walks about as the leader. Before counting any damage, it says what vanished from public life: shame and right living. Second, who was pushed aside: the qazis and the brahmins, the religious officials of both communities, have lost their place. Third, who suffered, and it doesn't stop at one side. The Muslim women read their scripture and in their pain cry out to Khuda, God. Women of the Hindu castes, high and low, are counted in the same reckoning. Yesterday Tilang spoke in the words of Muslim neighbors; here, in the same raga, grief crosses the same line. Nobody's suffering is left out to make a point. Fourth, when. Near its close, on the next page, Guru Nanak says he speaks the word of truth, and will tell the truth at the time of truth. That's the answer to the hook's question. Not when it's comfortable, and not only when someone powerful asks. When it's true, and the time has come. That's truth to power: the power never gets a vote on the timing. Whatever followed, the shabad was sung, kept and set in the Granth, where it is still sung in Tilang.
screen: `MODESTY AND DHARMA HAVE HIDDEN.` · `THE QAZIS AND BRAHMINS PUSHED ASIDE.` · `GRIEF ON EVERY SIDE IS COUNTED.` · `TRUTH AT THE TIME OF TRUTH.` · then, large: `TRUTH TO POWER.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, listen to this hymn, often searched as jaisee mai aavai khasam kee baanee, or let one true thing come to mind that you haven't said yet; it might be small. Shape it into one plain sentence, without blame and without softening, and simply hold it, with no need to say it today, and with one Waheguru if you pray.
A hymn in Tilang. Guru Nanak's song to Lalo about the invasion: what vanished, who was pushed aside, who grieved, and truth told at the time of truth. Today's word.
Your line: truth to power. Truth at the time of truth, kind as well as true. That's today, done.

1094.title: Raga Suhi
1094.hook: a raga of union and weddings that opens with a clean vessel, a pot of milk and a churn
1094.howItsDone: Shabads from the Suhi section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in kirtan in Raga Suhi, and because Suhi holds the Lavan, the raga is heard at the Anand Karaj, the Sikh wedding.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Tilang, sung to Lalo. Your line: truth to power.

A steel pot on the kitchen counter, a dish towel over the lid, left alone for the night. Warm milk went in, then a spoonful of yesterday's yogurt. By morning the two have become one thing, thick and set, and nobody can pull them apart again. Punjabi kitchens know that pot, and so does the Guru Granth Sahib. Today's raga is tied by tradition to weddings and union, and its very first hymn isn't about a bride at all. It's about the pot. Today: Raga Suhi.
screen: `A POT LEFT FOR THE NIGHT.` → `TWO BECOME ONE THING.` → `A RAGA OF UNION OPENS IN A KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. Suhi follows Tilang in the Granth's order, opening on ang seven twenty-eight. Sikh tradition links it with union and weddings, and its pages hold songs of the bride and the beloved; tomorrow opens some of them. Second, the kitchen. Guru Nanak's opening hymn, in paraphrase: wash the vessel, sit down, purify it with incense, and only then go out for the milk. The milk is your deeds. Awareness is the culture you stir in. And set it free of craving for a reward. Third, the refrain: chant the one Name; every other work bears no fruit. Fourth, the churn. Make this mind the handles, and staying awake the cord. Let the tongue repeat the Name, and churn like that: this is how the nectar is found. Why would a raga of union begin here? Milk and culture become one only in a clean pot, left in peace, with nobody poking at it to see if it's ready. The hymn describes union the way a cook does: prepare the vessel, bring something good, add a little of what's alive, and wait without grasping. Then the churning, the patient work that brings out what was hidden. Some readers hear the soul and God becoming one. Others hear a plain daily discipline. Both start with the same instruction: wash the pot first. Union.
screen: `SUHI FOLLOWS TILANG.` · `WASH THE VESSEL, THEN FETCH THE MILK.` · `CHANT THE ONE NAME.` · `THE MIND AS THE CHURN'S HANDLES.` · then, large: `UNION.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, play a shabad in Raga Suhi, or simply let the breath slow. For a minute, wash the pot, letting go of whatever is still sloshing around from today, one thing at a time; then leave it be, without checking whether it's working, like milk left to set, with Waheguru as the one word you stir in if you pray, or the breath alone if you don't.
Raga Suhi. The raga after Tilang, linked by tradition with weddings and union, which opens with a clean vessel, milk, a little culture and a churn. Today's word.
Your line: union. A clean pot, left in peace, with something alive stirred in. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1095.title: A hymn in Suhi
1095.hook: Suhi holds the Lavan, and Guru Nanak's paired poems of the unskilled and the skilled bride
1095.howItsDone: Guru Nanak's Kuchaji and Suchaji are sung in kirtan in Raga Suhi, and some Sikh teachers use them to explain bhana, acceptance of God's will; the Lavan in the same raga are sung at the Anand Karaj.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Suhi, which opens with a clean vessel, milk and a churn. Your line: union.

Skills. Job applications ask for them, dating profiles hint at them, and family weddings have their own unwritten list: can she cook, can he earn, will they fit in. In the Suhi section of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak sets two poems side by side. One is called Kuchaji, the unskilled bride. The next is Suchaji, the skilled bride. And the skill that wins the second poem its name is on nobody's list. Today: a hymn in Suhi.
screen: `CAN SHE COOK, CAN HE EARN.` → `TWO POEMS SIDE BY SIDE.` → `A SKILL ON NOBODY'S LIST.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. Suhi holds the Lavan, the four rounds that marry a Sikh couple; you walked them earlier on this path. Near them sit poems where the bride is the soul and the husband is the Lord. Second, the unskilled bride. In paraphrase: I'm unskilled, with faults beyond counting; how can I go to my Husband? The other brides seem each one better than the next; who would even know my name? The friends who have enjoyed their Lord sit in the shade of the mango trees. I have none of their virtues. It's a list of failures, said out loud, without dressing it up. Third, the skilled bride, and the surprise. She doesn't list talents. In paraphrase: when you are with me, I have everyone; you, my Master, are all my wealth. With you within, I live in peace. Then the line that turns the poem: by your will come thrones and greatness, and by your will a beggar's wandering. She isn't skilled because life went well. She can say the same thing on a throne and with a begging bowl: whatever comes, you are my wealth. Fourth, together. The poems hand out no prizes for beauty, wit or cooking. The unskilled bride's honesty about her faults is where the path begins. The skilled bride's skill is acceptance of the Lord's will, which Sikhs call bhana. That's the skilled bride.
screen: `SUHI HOLDS THE LAVAN.` · `KUCHAJI: I'M UNSKILLED, FULL OF FAULTS.` · `SUCHAJI: YOU ARE MY WEALTH.` · `THRONE OR BEGGING BOWL, BY YOUR WILL.` · then, large: `THE SKILLED BRIDE.`

segments.voice: Let one fault come to mind, plainly, the way the unskilled bride names hers, without a speech of excuses. Then set beside it one thing in your life that's going well and one that isn't, and hold them both in open hands, the throne and the bowl, with one Waheguru over both if you pray, or simply side by side if you don't.
A hymn in Suhi. Guru Nanak's paired poems: Kuchaji, the bride who names her faults, and Suchaji, whose skill is to say you are my wealth on a throne or with a bowl. Today's word.
Your line: the skilled bride. On a throne or with a bowl: you are my wealth. See you tomorrow.

1096.title: Raga Bilaval
1096.hook: a morning raga of joy that opens with a praise-singer admitting his words are too small, and singing on
1096.howItsDone: Shabads from the Bilaval section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in kirtan in Raga Bilaval, which Sikh musical tradition links with the morning and a joyful mood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Suhi: two brides, one who names her faults and one who says you are my wealth. Your line: the skilled bride.

Calling a king sir is not a compliment. It's a downgrade. Sir is what you call the man at the next table, and leaving off a king's bigger titles is a little insult, however politely it's meant. Now turn to where a new raga begins in the Guru Granth Sahib. Guru Nanak opens it with exactly that problem: every title he has is too small for the One he's singing to. And he sings on anyway. Today: Raga Bilaval.
screen: `CALLING A KING SIR.` → `EVERY TITLE TOO SMALL.` → `AND SINGS ON ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Bilaval follows Suhi in the Granth's order. Sikh tradition, along with the wider music it grew from, links Bilaval with morning and joy. Second, the opening line, in paraphrase: you are the Sultan; if I call you Mian, sir, what greatness is that? Mian was a respectful title in Guru Nanak's world. Beside the One who made everything, it's like calling the ocean a puddle. Third, the confession. Whatever you give, Master, that is what I say; I'm a fool, I can't find the words. Then the refrain, a request: give me understanding, so I can sing your praises and live in truth, by your will. Then: whatever has happened has come from you; you know everything. I can't know your limit, my Master; what cleverness do I have? I speak and speak, and see that the one beyond words can't be put into words. Whatever pleases you, I say, and it's a sesame seed of your greatness. Fourth, the joy. A praise song that keeps admitting it can't praise might sound like defeat. But it doesn't stop; it asks for understanding to keep singing, in a raga tradition links with joy. There's freedom in it. Nobody has to find the perfect word, because it doesn't exist. So the morning song can start with a small one, sir, smile at how small it is, and still be sung gladly. Morning joy.

segments.voice: Choose something larger than you, the sky this morning, the ocean, the fact that you woke up at all, and try to describe it in a few words in your head. Notice how small the words are and let it be a little funny, the way sir is funny for a sultan; then let the words go and enjoy the thing itself, with one Waheguru if you pray, or a small smile if you don't.

1097.title: A hymn in Bilaval
1097.hook: Bilaval holds Guru Arjan's song of shelter from the hot wind, sung after the danger has passed
1097.howItsDone: Guru Arjan's Bilaval shabad taatee vaao na lagaee is sung in kirtan and recited by Sikhs for protection and in thanks, at times of illness and recovery, before journeys and at births.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Bilaval, where Guru Nanak calls the Sultan sir and sings on gladly. Your line: morning joy.

The storm blew all night. In the morning someone opens the front door and steps out to look: branches down, the street wet, the house still standing. Somebody puts the kettle on. Somebody laughs at nothing. Somebody cries, and it isn't sad crying. Relief has a sound, and it's closer to joy than to quiet. Today's hymn, in the raga opened yesterday, sounds like that doorway after the storm. Today: a hymn in Bilaval.
screen: `THE STORM HAS PASSED.` → `RELIEF HAS A SOUND.` → `A HYMN THAT SOUNDS LIKE IT.`

segments.voice: First, the song. Bilaval holds hymns of Guru Arjan about shelter, and one of them, on ang eight nineteen, begins taatee vaao na lagaee: the hot wind doesn't touch the one in the refuge of the Supreme Lord. Earlier on this path you opened its pictures: the scorching wind, the refuge, the protective line drawn on four sides. Today, listen for the tense. Second, the verbs. In paraphrase: I met the perfect Guru, who arranged all this. He gave the medicine of the Lord's Name. The Protector protected me and erased every illness. Grace came, says Nanak, and God became my helper. Met, gave, protected, erased, came. Nearly all of it already happened. This isn't a plea shouted into the storm. It's a song sung after the wind has dropped. Third, the story people tell. Some Sikh tellers link Guru Arjan's Bilaval hymns of this kind to a time when his young son Hargobind fell ill and recovered. The hymn names no one, so hold that as tradition, not as the text. Fourth, why a raga of joy. Shelter and joy are two halves of one moment. Fear runs ahead of the danger; thanks runs behind it. Guru Arjan set that relief in Bilaval, the raga tradition links with morning joy, so the thanks would be sung, not just felt. Joy and shelter.
screen: `THE HOT WIND DOESN'T TOUCH.` · `MET, GAVE, PROTECTED, ERASED.` · `A STORY OF A SON WHO RECOVERED.` · `THANKS RUNS BEHIND THE DANGER.` · then, large: `JOY AND SHELTER.`

segments.voice: Bring back one time something passed that you feared wouldn't, an illness, a bad night, a test result, and skip the fear: go straight to the moment after, when it was over. Feel where the relief sits in the body now, the chest, the shoulders, the face, and stay there, with one Waheguru as thanks if you pray, or the relief as the whole of it if you don't.
A hymn in Bilaval. Guru Arjan's song of shelter from the hot wind, told mostly in the past tense: the danger passed, and the thanks is sung in a raga of joy. Today's word.

1098.title: Raga Gond
1098.hook: a raga where a weaver, a cloth printer and a leatherworker sing beside the Gurus
1098.howItsDone: Hymns of the Bhagats, such as Kabir, Namdev and Ravidas, are sung in kirtan from the Guru Granth Sahib alongside the Gurus' hymns, and Sikhs bow to the whole Granth, Bhagat bani included, as the Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Bilaval, the hot wind passing and the thanks sung after. Your line: joy and shelter.

A weaver. A cloth printer. A leatherworker. That's how tradition remembers Kabir, Namdev and Ravidas: by their work, in a world where, tradition says, such work kept people far from the front of the temple. Now open the Guru Granth Sahib to the raga after Bilaval. Their hymns are there, under the same heading as the Gurus', sung to the same raga, bowed to in the same book. Today: Raga Gond.
screen: `A WEAVER, A PRINTER, A LEATHERWORKER.` → `REMEMBERED BY THEIR WORK.` → `THE SAME HEADING AS THE GURUS.`

segments.voice: Gond opens with Guru Ram Das, and one of his first lines is worth carrying, in paraphrase: the Lord knows everything that happens inside a person, and lets not even a sesame seed's worth of anyone's effort go to waste. Second, the Bhagats: the Sikh name for the devotional poets, not Gurus themselves, whose hymns the Gurus set beside their own. Gond makes room for them: Kabir the weaver, Namdev, Ravidas. Third, two of their voices. Namdev, in paraphrase: great sacrifices, giving away your weight in gold, bathing where the holy rivers meet at Prayag, none of these equals singing the Lord's praise. Ravidas, in paraphrase: Mukand, Mukand, the Liberator; chant that name, world, for without the Liberator the body comes to nothing. Neither argues for his own importance. They point past themselves, and past every ceremony, to the Name. Fourth, why it matters. A scripture is a list of who gets heard. The Gurus could have kept their book to their own line. Instead they made room for a weaver and a leatherworker, and Gond is one place you hear them. That's why it's called the bhagats' raga here. Guru Ram Das's line reads differently now: not a sesame seed of anyone's effort wasted. Not a weaver's, either.

1099.title: A hymn in Gond
1099.hook: Gond holds Kabir's song of the elephant that would not charge, and the judge who still didn't see
1099.howItsDone: Kabir's Gond hymn of the elephant is sung in kirtan from the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teachers retell it as a story of the devotee protected by the Lord, whose strength the refrain names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Gond, where a weaver, a cloth printer and a leatherworker sing beside the Gurus. Your line: the bhagats' raga. This week ends today: Lalo's hymn, Suhi's brides, Bilaval's joy, and Gond.

Three look at the same thing and see three different things. A judge sees a troublemaker who has to be made an example of. A driver sees an order he can't refuse, and a threat against his own life. And an elephant, huge and goaded, looks down at a man tied up in a bundle and sees something neither of the others can. You met this hymn of Kabir's earlier on the path. This time, watch the eyes. Today: a hymn in Gond.
screen: `THREE WHO LOOK.` → `A JUDGE, A DRIVER, AN ELEPHANT.` → `WATCH THE EYES.`

segments.voice: First, the refrain, the line the whole hymn turns on, on ang eight seventy. In paraphrase: O my Lord, the strength is yours. Kabir doesn't say the elephant was gentle, or that he was clever. He sets the whole story under that line. Second, the driver. The judge, the qazi, shouts at him: drive it on, or I'll cut you to pieces; goad it, beat it. The driver strikes the elephant on the head. He sees an order and a threat, and obeys. The hymn doesn't curse him. It shows a man too frightened to see anything else. Third, the elephant. It runs off crying out, and Kabir hears it say: I am a sacrifice to this form. Then it stands still, in meditation, because the Lord dwells in its heart. It lifts the bundle again and again, and bows. Fourth, the judge. Kabir asks him plainly: what wrong has this saint done, that you tied him up and gave him to the elephant? The verdict is about eyes: the qazi, in his darkness, didn't understand. Three times, the hymn says, he put it to the test, and his hard heart still wasn't convinced. Seeing isn't only about what's in front of you. It's about the heart doing the looking. The judge looked straight at a wonder and saw nothing, while the beast he meant as a weapon saw the Lord. The elephant bowed.
screen: `THE STRENGTH IS YOURS, MY LORD.` · `THE DRIVER SEES AN ORDER.` · `THE ELEPHANT SEES THE LORD, AND BOWS.` · `THE JUDGE STILL DOESN'T SEE.` · then, large: `THE ELEPHANT BOWED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you've already made up your mind about, someone you see as a problem, though not someone who has harmed you, and hold their face. Then slowly look at them the way the elephant looked at the bundle on the ground: not as a target or an order, but as someone the Lord might live inside; you don't have to change your mind, just look once more, with one Waheguru if you pray.
A hymn in Gond. Kabir's song of the elephant that would not charge: a frightened driver, a judge who didn't see, and a refrain that says the strength is yours. Today's word.
Your line: the elephant bowed. A second look can see what the first one missed. Another week, done.
